title: The morning Shema
hook: the Shema in the morning, even just the first line
tomorrow: one blessing before a meal. why does the Torah ask for one after?

segments.voice: Yesterday, washing: water over each hand, and then the first move is yours. A clean start. Hands washed; now, a line said morning and night.

Earbuds in before breakfast: a podcast, a playlist, a voice telling you what to think about the day. The morning starts by listening to something, and usually to several things at once: a news alert, the group chat, a song stuck in your head from last night. One question for today: what should a day start by listening for? Jews have answered with the same line, morning and night, for a very long time. And the first thing it asks you to do isn't to believe, or to act. It's to hear.
screen: `EARBUDS IN BEFORE BREAKFAST.` → `WHAT SHOULD A DAY LISTEN FOR?` → `FIRST, HEAR.`

segments.voice: The line is from Deuteronomy: "Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one." In Hebrew, the first word is Shema, hear, and the whole passage takes its name from it. A few verses later comes the instruction to speak these words "when thou liest down, and when thou risest up." So the Shema bookends the day, morning and night. The Talmud tells that Rabbi Judah the Prince covered his eyes when he said the first line, and Jews still do it: eyes covered, the world shut out for one sentence, nothing to look at, only something to hear. Even the first line alone, said in the morning with meaning, is a beginning. Now a neighbor who says something close. Muslims recite a short chapter of the Qur'an, Surah al-Ikhlas, which in Pickthall's translation opens: "Say: He is Allah, the One!" Shared ground: God's oneness, said aloud, in words people carry by heart. And an honest difference, right in the first word. The Shema opens with hear, a call to a people, Israel, to listen together. Al-Ikhlas opens with say, a declaration the Qur'an gives the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, to proclaim. One begins by listening; the other by speaking. Each tradition reads its own line in its own way, and neither needs the other's to be the same. For a Jewish morning, the order matters: before you say anything, hear. Hear, every morning.
screen: `HEAR, O ISRAEL.` · `WHEN THOU LIEST DOWN, AND RISEST UP.` · `EYES COVERED, ONE SENTENCE.` · `SAY: HE IS ALLAH, THE ONE.` · then, large: `HEAR, EVERY MORNING.`

segments.voice: Cover your eyes with one hand, the way people do for the Shema's first line. If you say it, say it once, slowly, out loud or in a whisper: Shema Yisrael. If not, simply listen, eyes covered, to whatever you can hear around you for the rest of the sit. Let one sound at a time have your whole attention.
screen: `ONE HAND OVER THE EYES.` · `SHEMA, SLOWLY.` · `OR JUST LISTEN.`

segments.voice: The morning Shema: hear, O Israel, said as the day begins, often with the eyes covered. Listening first.
Your line: hear, every morning. Listen before you say a word. Day one thousand six hundred fifty-one.

screen: `DAY 1651 COUNTS.` → `LIVING IT · 4 OF 130.` → `TOMORROW: A BLESSING BEFORE. WHY ONE AFTER, TOO?`

howItsDone: Jews say the Shema in the morning and evening prayers and at bedtime, covering the eyes for the first line; the first line is also among the first prayers Jewish children learn.
